INTRODUCTION
1
Preface
In this booklet, you will find an overview of the postgraduate research projects currently being undertaken
by PhD candidates and postdocs working in the various groups of the Debye Institute for Nanomaterials
Science of Utrecht University (Debye Institute) and the Institute for Sustainable and Circular Chemistry
(ISCC). This booklet not only serves as an interesting overview of the scientific work to which these
institutes are associated, but also as an easy means with which to encourage collaboration between 7
the different research groups. Each contribution consists of a brief summary of the work performed,
with the most important aspects of the research project highlighted in the header and keywords. At
the back of the booklet, you will find both the author index and the technique index. The author index
lists all names of the PhD candidates and postdocs of the Debye Institute and the ISCC. The technique
index summarizes the most commonly used spectroscopic, experimental and computational techniques
used by each research group, including the name and contact details of the responsible staff member
for each technique. This year’s technique index also features the Electron Microscopy Centre (EMC)
as part of the Faculty of Science. The EMC provides valuable tools to perform a variety of microscopic-
and spectroscopic methods and could be relevant to many people in our institutes.
This book has been composed by the members of the Debye PhD Committee (Debye AiO Commissie,
DAC), which is a representative body for the PhD candidates and postdocs of the Debye institute. This
edition of the Debye and ISCC Booklet contains contributions for 137 postgraduate research projects.
New in this edition of the booklet is the fact that now two institutes are contributing. The Inorganic
Chemistry and Catalysis group (ICC) and the Organic Chemistry and Catalysis group (OCC) started a
new institute in September 2022, the Institute for Sustainable and Circular Chemistry. The ICC group
has opted for a double affiliation, and is thus also still a member of the Debye Institute. One might say
the two institutes form a Venn diagram with the ICC occupying the middle section. We see this mitosis
as a sign of continued growth and hope to see many fruitful collaborations in the future.
Happy researching!
On behalf of the DAC,
Bram Verreussel

1 INTRODUCTION
Debye Institute for Nanomaterials Sciences
Around the central theme “Nanomaterials for Sustainability,” the Debye Institute performs research
in three interconnected areas that are relevant to the transition to a sustainable society, namely,
• Catalysis and Energy Materials,
• Nanophotonics and Quantum Materials, and
• Colloids and Biomaterials.
Six research groups from the departments of Chemistry and Physics carry out these themes: Condensed
Matter and Interfaces (CMI), Materials Chemistry and Catalysis (MCC), Inorganic Chemistry and
Catalysis (ICC), Nanophotonics (NP), Soft Condensed Matter and Biophysics (SCMB), and Van ‘t Hoff
Laboratory for Physical and Colloid Chemistry (PCC).
Our mission is to perform research at the highest level, integrating experiments, theory, and simulations
in a multidisciplinary approach. We aim to create knowledge relevant to sustainability and health and
to provide high-level education for MSc students and PhD candidates in a stimulating environment
that fosters collaboration.

Institute for Sustainable and Circular Chemistry
The Institute for Sustainable and Circular Chemistry was founded by members from the research
groups Inorganic Chemistry and Catalysis (ICC) and Organic Chemistry and Catalysis (OCC), and by
members of the Utrecht Hub of the Advanced Research Center Chemical Building Blocks Consortium
(ARC CBBC). Research at the ISCC focuses at “closing element loops” using clean, energy-efficient and
resource-efficient conversion and manufacturing processes. These processes should then yield products
that are both circular-by-design and safe-by-design. This can only be achieved by molecular redesign
and the adoption of a systems approach to chemistry, including end-of-life studies (environmental
impact) and related risk assessment. This research requires much interdisciplinary collaboration,
which is achieved through collaboration with toxicologists as well as technoeconomic and life cycle
analysts. We believe in training and educating a new generation of chemists by giving them a strong
foundation in chemistry, coupled with the ability and curiosity to look across the boundaries of
science and to connect different disciplines. Both through research and education, we aim to reinvent
chemistry for a sustainable future.

The Debye PhD Committee (DAC)
The Debye PhD Committee (Debye AiO Commissie) exists in order to represent the interests of all the
different researchers currently working within the Debye Institute. Each research group is represented
by at least one PhD candidate. Together, the DAC unites the various research groups by organizing
activities like the Debye Sports Day at the beginning of each academic year, the social events during the
Debye Spring School and the Debye Introduction Afternoon (DIM) for new PhD students and postdocs.
The DAC also contributes to the educational programme by organizing the biannual career-oriented
Debye DO! Days event, where PhD candidates have the chance to discuss future career moves with
employees across a broad scope of science-orientated jobs. If you have any questions regarding the DAC,
the Debye Institute, or any upcoming events, please do not hesitate to contact the DAC representative
of your group. A list of the current DAC members is provided below. We would also like to mention
previous members Kirsten Siebers (ICC), Marjolein de Jager (SCMB) and Matthijs Alting (PCC), who
left during the creation of this booklet.

ISCC PhD and PD Activity Committee (IPAC)
The PhD and PD Activity Committee (IPAC) represents PhD candidates and postdocs working within
the Institute for Sustainable and Circular Chemistry (ISCC). It consists of four members, two from
the Organic Chemistry and Catalysis (OCC) and two from the Inorganic Chemistry and Catalysis (ICC)
research group. The IPAC communicates matters from PhD candidates and postdocs to the ISCC board
and vice versa, also in cooperation with the PhD candidate within the ISCC board. Furthermore, the
IPAC assists with the institute newsletter and organizes events, both social and work related. Next to
that, the IPAC organizes the social part of the Spring School, and the Sports Day, together with the DAC
from the Debye Institute. If you have any questions, don’t hesitate to contact us at ipac.iscc@uu.nl.

Research Mission
The CMI group investigates the relation between the atomic structure of (low-dimensional) materials
and their electronic, optical, magnetic and superconductive properties. The research includes material
synthesis, structural characterization, several methods of optical, electrical and magnetic microscopy
and spectroscopy combined with first-principles theory and simulations.

Investigating Nanomagnets on Superconductors with
Shot-Noise STM
Jan Cuperus (PhD), j.p.cuperus@uu.nl
Sponsor: ERC
Supervisors: prof. dr. D. Vanmaekelbergh, dr. Ingmar Swart
Superconductivity, Shot-noise, Scanning tunneling microscopy
Today’s electronic devices suffer from a considerable loss of energy in the form of heat. With the ever
increasing scale of information processing, it is essential to develop devices that are more efficient
– either in power usage or in information processing. In both cases, new materials are required to
enable this. In particular, there is a broad interest in topological superconductivity – a state of matter
that may open the part towards topological quantum computing.
In condensed matter systems, topological superconductivity can be realized by the combination of
magnetism and ‘normal’ superconductivity. This was recently shown for 1D atomic chains [1] and
2D islands.[2] However, in both cases the smoking gun evidence is lacking. In my research, I hope to
increase the general understanding of low-dimensional nanomagnets on superconductors.
The key technique I am using is the scanning tunneling microscope (STM). Using an STM,
12 the surfaces of semi-, normal and superconductors can be investigated both physically and
electronically. Moreover, the extreme resolution of the STM (sub-pm) can be used to alter the
structure of a surface atom-by-atom. Recently, the toolbox of STM was expanded by the addition of
shot-noise spectroscopy.[3] I will be using all these capabilities of STM to investigate the dynamics
and interactions of nanomagnets on superconducting substrates, in particular Fe adatoms and CrCl3
nanosheets on NbSe2.
Figure 1: a) LDOS mapping of an atomic chain of Fe atoms on a Pb substrate. Increased intensity is observed at 0 V, indicative
of topological superconductivity.[1] b) Schematic of the 2D magnet CrBr3 with the superconductor NbSe2. [2]
[1] S. Nadj-Perge et al., Science, (346), pp. 602-607, 2014.
[2] S. Kezilebieke et al., Nature, (588), pp. 424-428, 2020.
[3] K. Bastiaans et al., Rev. Sci. Instr., (89), pp. 93709, 2018.

Bi-ene/X Interfaces and Their Effects
Montserrat Navarro Espino (PhD), m.navarroespino@uu.nl
Sponsor: QuMat
Supervisor(s): dr. Zeila Zanolli, prof. dr. Cristiane de Morais Smith,
dr. Andrés Botello Méndez
Density Functional Theory, 2D Heterostructures, Proximity Effects
In recent years, van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures have gained a lot of popularity in the field
of condensed matter. These structures consist of layered materials of different types (TMDCs, TIs,
SC, etc.) characterized by extended crystalline planar structures, held together by strong in-plane
covalent bonds and weak out-of-plane vdW forces.[1] Since new properties emerge in the interface
of the layers, a variety of potential applications opens, for example, the design of ultrafast and low-
power electronic and spintronic devices [2][3], among others.
This project will focus on studying the atomic structure of the interface of bismuthene with a
substrate or with another layered material, and how strain and other proximity effects affect the
topological band structure. DFT calculations will be combined with other theoretical methods
(e.g. semi-empirical tight-binding) to obtain realistic band structures. We will seek tendencies to
optimize the topological gap and take care of chemical stability. Building on the results obtained 13
using the theoretical methods mentioned previously, electronic transport simulations will be
performed in a disordered system using the Kwant code [4] to prove that the conducting states are
robust against disorder. By studying these systems from first principles simulations and exploring
the quantum transport in them, we will develop the capability to push the condensed matter field
further and translate scientific achievements into technology that exploits quantum phenomena.[5]
[1] Ajayan et al., Physics Today, (69), pp. 38-44, 2016.
[2] Sierra et al., Nature Nanoletters, (16), pp. 856-868, 2021.
[3] Geim et al., Nature, (499), pp. 419-425, 2013.
[4] Groth et al., New Journal of Physics, (16), pp. 01-39, 2014.
[5] Montblanch et al., Nature Nanoletters, (18), pp. 555-571, 2023.

Topological Superconductivity from First-Principles
Arnold Herman Kole (PhD), a.h.kole@uu.nl
Sponsor: Sector Plan 2019
Supervisor(s): dr. Zeila Zanolli, dr. Ingmar Swart
Superconductivity, Topology, Density Functional Theory
In recent years there has been an increased interest in materials with topological properties. These
materials are characterised by a topological phase, which is separated from the normal phase by
a discontinuous transformation. Topological phases and their related properties are therefore
protected from disorder. Topological superconductors are a subclass of topological materials
where a superconducting material exhibits a topological phase. They might exhibit exciting new
forms of physics such as edge states that behave like Majorana fermions.[1] One route to topological
superconductivity could be by creating hybrid structures that combine s-wave superconductivity
with spin-orbit coupling and magnetism.[1] Examples include structures where chains of
magnetic atoms (Fe, Mn) are put on top of superconducting subtrates (Nb, Re) or Van der Waals
heterostructures of superconductors (NbSe2) and two-dimensional magnetic materials (CrX3
14 where X=Cl,Br,I). Experiments show in-gap states in these materials which might be a signature
of topological superconductivity.[2-4] Attempts have been made to explain these experiments using
theoretical models, but a treatment that combines superconductivity with the full complexity of
the electronic state of these systems is still missing. We have recently implemented an approach to
describe superconductivity through the Bogoliubov-deGennes formalism in the Density Functional
Theory code SIESTA.[5,6] The advantage of this unified approach is that material specific properties
are treated accurately, such as the gap anisotropy for bulk Niobium that can be seen in Figure 1. We
use this state-of-the-art method to understand the physics behind these in-gap states and help
elucidate their origin. A better understanding will allow us to make predictions about new materials
that can host these states and perhaps eventually allows us to tune their properties.

Fe(Se,Te) / topological insulator hybrids: growth and
characterization
Floris Kooij (PhD), f.m.kooij@uu.nl
Sponsor: NWO, ERC
Supervisor(s): dr. Ingmar Swart, prof. dr. Guus Rijnders (UTwente)
Topological superconductivity, scanning probe microscopy
Within condensed matter physics, there is widespread interest in topologically non-trivial materials
and associated topologically protected states. In topological superconductors, these theoretically
include Majorana quasiparticles, manifesting as zero-bound states living within the superconducting
gap. Besides fundamental interests, such modes are attractive candidates for topological quantum
computing due to them obeying non-Abelian statistics.[1]
Recently, potential Majorana zero-bound modes have been observed in, among others, vortex cores
and in grain boundaries in bulk Fe(Se, Te) (FST) single crystals[2, 3], and in single-unit cell FST films
grown on a SrTiO3 substrate.[4] Here, the latter is of particular interest considering the remarkably
high superconducting critical temperature compared to the bulk. However, the topological nature of
the observed states is not definitively established due to different effects mimicking the zero-bound
mode characteristics. 15
In this joint project between the universities of Utrecht and Twente, we aim to grow said FST crystals
on well-defined substrates, i.e. SrTiO3 and other crystalline oxides. We wish to control the thickness
of the FST system, the atomic registry of the interface, the lateral size of the FST crystal domains,
and the presence of defects. The electronic structure of these systems, including the superconducting
gap and the zero-bound states living within, will be studied using state-of-the-art scanning
tunneling microscopy. Here, we employ directional magnetic fields and high-frequency shot noise
measurements at temperatures down to 330 mK. If possible, we will employ atomic manipulation to
engineer defect states beyond naturally-occurring Se/Te line defects, and study its influence on the
zero-bound states.
[1] Nayak et al., Rev. Mod. Phys., (80), pp. 83–1159, 2008.
[2] Wang et al., Science, (362), pp. 333-335, 2018.
[3] Zhang et al., Science, (360), pp. 182-186, 2018.
[4] Chen et al., Nat. Phys., (16), pp. 536–540, 2020.

Correlated electron systems studied with local shot-noise
measurements
Maialen Ortego Larrazabal (PhD), m.ortegolarrazabal@uu.nl
Sponsor: NWO
Supervisor(s): dr. Ingmar Swart
Scanning tunneling microscopy, Superconductivity, Shot-noise
Many aspects of condensed matter physics seek to understand how order emerges when a
very large number of simpler components, such as electrons, interact with each other. In
the general case, it is not always possible to study systems of interacting electrons directly,
due to their complexity. My research is focused on the study of the electronic properties of quantum
materials, such as superconductors, using a newly developed experimental technique that combines
scanning tunnelling microscopy with shot-noise spectroscopy. This method can probe the effective
charge of the carriers in the nanoscale, giving us information about the electronic correlations locally.

Electronic Designer Quantum Materials Created Atom-by-Atom
Rian Ligthart (PhD), r.a.m.ligthart@uu.nl
Sponsor: ERC Consolidator Grant, started in October 2020
Supervisor(s): dr. Ingmar Swart, prof. dr. Daniël Vanmaekelbergh
Designer Quantum Materials, Artificial Electronic Lattices, Scanning
Tunneling Microscopy (STM)
Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) can be used for imaging with atomic resolution, probing
electronic properties and moving single atoms with nano-scale precision. The STM is, therefore,
a suitable technique for building artificial electronic lattices that function as a quantum simulator
to create designer quantum materials. A quantum simulator is created by confining the surface
state electrons with attractive or repulsive scatterers on the surface, resulting in particle-in-
a-box like states. These states can be considered as artificial atoms and used to build dimers,
1D chains and more complex crystal lattices. The artificial atoms are formed by manipulating
single atoms over a surface through vertical or lateral manipulation, see Figure 1. The atomic
precision with which the atoms can be moved allows to create designer quantum materials.
The versatile electronic lattices are used to study the effect of structure on electronic characteristics,
thereby functioning as quantum simulator. Recently, CO molecules on Cu(111) were used to build (i) 17
molecular graphene [1] creating massless fermions in a Dirac cone, (ii) the Sierpiński triangle [2] where
the electrons behaved like they were in a fractal dimension of 1.58 and (iii) a topological insulators
such as the Kekulé lattice [3] were a robust edge mode was realized. In this project, the energy
resolution of the CO/Cu(111) system is aimed to improve by moving the lattices to a semiconductor
surface. The electronic states of the designer material will fall into the bandgap of the semiconductor
preventing the coupling to bulk states. So far, new systems for the artificial electronic lattices have
been realized using In or Cs atoms on InAs(111)A. Briefly, in this project new systems that function as
quantum simulator are studied and when suitable used to probe novel effects in the quantum world!
Figure 1: a) Schematic of procedure of vertical manipulation which consists of picking up a single
adatom on a surface and putting down b)-d) STM image of Cs atoms on InAs(111)A where a Cs is
picked up by the tip b) and no longer on the surface c) to subsequently be dropped at a given
position d). e) Schematic of the procedure of lateral manipulation where an adatom is moving
over the surface without breaking the bond between adatom and surface. f)-g) STM image of
a Cs atom being moved over the surface by overcoming the diffusion barrier mediated by the tip.

[2] Kempkes, S. N., Slot. M. R.., Nature Physics, (2), pp. 127-131, 2019.
[3] Freeney, S.E.., Physical Review Letters, (23), pp. 236404, 2020.

First-principles methods for superconducting and optical properties
of quantum materials
Riccardo Reho (PhD), r.reho@uu.nl
Sponsor: Sector Plan 2019-2024
Supervisor(s): dr. Zeila Zanolli
Theoretical spectroscopy, 2D heterostructures, Superconductivity
I specialize in formulating and developing theoretical frameworks to elucidate quantum phenomena in
materials, including superconductivity and light-matter interaction. My contribution in spectroscopy
focuses on examining the optical properties of two-dimensional (2D) multilayer structures formed
by Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) and topological insulators like Bi2Se3. These multilayer
2D structures enhance the Coulomb interaction between charge carriers leading to strongly bound
electron-hole (exciton) pairs. The physics of these excitons are both of fundamental interest and
of crucial importance for engineering and exploiting the properties of these materials in potential
applications, for example, in photovoltaic devices where the silicon era has reached its efficiency
limit. My research revealed a pronounced excitonic shift due to twisting and strain for MoS2/WS2 and
MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. .For the analysis of the optical spectra of these systems I implemented
18 a method for computing the Photoluminescence (PL) spectra using the YAMBO code.[1,2]
Moreover, in collaboration with the group of D. Vanmaekelbergh, we have discovered that the higher-
energy surface excitations in a 6 Quintuple Layer of Bi2Se3 are distinctive, preserving the polarization
of incident light, which results in the creation of chiral excitons .[3]
In the realm of superconductivity, I investigate both conventional superconductors, which are described
by the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory.[4] and function at extremely low temperatures, and
unconventional superconductors, which exhibit high-temperature superconductivity from non-
electron-phonon mechanisms. In the Quantum Materials by Design group we combined Bogoliubov-
de-Gennes and Density Functional Theory (DFT) in a unified approach, Superconducting Density
Functional Theory (SCDFT).[5,6], and extended it to unconventional superconductors. We implemented
and optimized a novel approach in the SIESTA code .[7,8]
I’ve applied this method to study complex heterostructures like PbTe/Pb, contributing evidence for
induced superconductivity through proximity effects.

Colloidal Garnet Nanocrystals for LEDs
Maaike van der Sluijs (Postdoc), m.m.vandersluijs@uu.nl
Sponsor: Seaborough
Supervisor(s): dr. Celso de Mello-Donega
Luminescence, YAG:Ce, Colloidal Nanocrystals
Y3Al5O12:Ce3+ (YAG:Ce) garnets have shown exceptional optical properties as microcrystalline and
single-crystalline materials. In addition, they have high chemical and thermal stability, making
them ideal for applications such as phosphors in white LEDs. However, their synthesis requires high
temperatures (≥1500 °C) and the formed particles have a large grain size. While many materials have
been developed on the nanoscale, with excellent optical properties (e.g., semiconductor quantum
dots, perovskite nanocrystals, and rare earth doped phosphors), synthesis methods for high-quality
colloidal garnet nanocrystals (NCs) are still lacking.[1] High-quality, freestanding, crystalline, high
quantum yield colloidal garnet NCs would be beneficial for many applications (biomedical tagging
and imaging, scintillators, high-efficiency solid-state lighting, micro-LEDs) and would allow low-
cost device preparation through solution-processing.
A promising synthesis method is the glycothermal synthesis, which takes place at temperatures 19
above the normal boiling points of the solvents, in a closed vessel at high autogenous pressures.
Under these conditions, crystalline YAG:Ce nanoparticles can be formed in one step at temperatures
as low as 250 °C. However, the synthesis of small (5-20 nm), free-standing colloidal YAG:Ce NCs
remains challenging, since the nanoparticles tend to aggregate and coalesce during the reaction.
Further development of the synthesis methods has been hindered by the poor understanding of the
reaction mechanisms, which have not yet been thoroughly investigated.[2][3]
The aim of this project is to develop wet-chemistry, low-temperature methods to synthesize high-
quality colloidal YAG:Ce NCs in the 10 to 100 nm size range. To this end, we aim to first unravel the
mechanisms involved in the formation of nanoscale YAG:Ce by combining several in-situ and ex-
situ techniques (TEM, XRD, optical spectroscopy, GC-MS, NMR, SAXS, WAXS, elemental analysis).
The acquired knowledge will be applied to develop synthesis methods to obtain YAG NCs with good
control over size (<50 nm) and shape. We expect additional improvements in the optical properties,
towards the levels reached by micron-scale YAG (i.e., near-unity QYs).
[1] A. C. Berends et al., Chemical Reviews, (120), pp. 13461-13479, 2020.
[2] M. Inoue et al., Journal of the American Ceramic Society, (74), pp. 1452-1454, 1991.
[3] P. Ramanujam et al., The Journal of Supercritical Fluids, (107), pp. 433-440, 2016.

Luminescent Semiconductor Nanocrystals for the Energy Transition
Raimon Terricabres-Polo (PhD), r.terricabrespolo@uu.nl
Sponsor: TKI Urban Energy
Supervisor(s): dr. Celso de Mello-Donega, prof. dr. Wilfried van Sark
Semiconductor Nanocrystals, Spectroscopy, Luminescent Solar
Concentrators
Generating energy from renewable sources is crucial for a sustainable future. One such example is
photovoltaic technologies, which convert sunlight into electricity. Despite the widespread use of
solar panels in rural and industrial landscapes, their deployment in cities is unfeasible because of land
scarcity. Unsurprisingly, energy consumption is the highest there. Luminescent solar concentrators
(LSCs) enable energy harvesting in this urban setting by substituting passive construction elements
like windows and glass facades. By means of a luminescent material, part of the light going through
the LSCs is concentrated at the edges, where it will be converted to electricity by a solar cell (Figure 1).
In my research, I synthesize luminescent semiconductor nanocrystals, characterize their
optoelectronic properties and use them to fabricate LSCs. By tuning the synthesis parameters, we
can control the bandgap of the nanocrystals to match the desired region of the solar spectrum.
20 We also make use of a broad range of spectroscopic techniques to characterize the absorption and
emission of light by the nanocrystals. Recently, we have looked into the long-term performance of

Topological insulators (TIs) are bulk insulators that host conductive states at their surface (in the
case of 3D materials) or edge (for 2D materials). The emergence of these states is related to the
material’s electronic band structure, where an inversion of the conduction and valence bands occurs
due to strong spin-orbit coupling. Consequently, the conductive states retain their metallic character
despite the presence of crystal disorder or impurities. This robustness, combined with exotic effects
such as spin-filtering, results in TIs being regarded as intriguing materials for material science,
nanoelectronics, and spintronics.[1]
Of the known TIs, Bi2Se3 is one of the most widely researched materials.[2,3] However, reports on the
electronic properties of Bi2Se3 nanoplatelets (NPLs) are surprisingly scarce. Because of their small
size, NPLs provide a unique opportunity to study the effects of quantum confinement on the NPLs’
22 opto-electronic properties. We therefore aim to synthesize colloidal Bi2Se3 NPLs and investigate
their properties using transient absorption spectroscopy, conductivity measurements, and scanning
tunneling spectroscopy/microscopy (STS/STM). In Figure 1, a TEM image of several Bi2Se3 NPLs is
shown. The LDOS(x,y) map of one platelet, also shown in Figure 1, shows that the edge states of these
NPLs can be visualized with STM.
In addition to synthesizing Bi2Se3 NPLs, we aim to develop new synthesis routes for colloidal
topological crystalline insulators (TCIs). TCIs constitute a subclass of TIs in which the surface
conductivity is protected by the point group symmetry of the crystal. Currently, we are using cation
exchange and one-pot synthesis techniques to obtain SnTe NPLs and nanocrystals of Pb1-x Snx Te
with tunable dimensions.

Quantum materials, Magnetism, Crystal growth
Van der Waals (vdW) materials are highly anisotropic materials consisting of layers bonded together
by weak vdW interactions, that allow for the possibility of these materials to be cleaved into very thin
specimens, down to atomically thin monolayers. Of particular contemporary interest are magnetic
vdW materials, as these materials provide the ideal platform for exploring magnetism in the 2D
limit, where new phenomena are expected.[1]
Magnetic order in 2D, which is associated with strong intrinsic spin fluctuations, can only happen
if there is no continuous rotational symmetry in the material, and low-energy modes are gapped
through magnetic anisotropy.[2, 3] Since anisotropy can be introduced into the magnetic system
through spin-orbit coupling or lattice distortions, the family of 2D vdW materials with magnetic
order is predicted to be rather large, and many novel materials are expected.[4]
In my research I focus on the synthesis and structural characterization of (new) compounds within 23
this rich family, as well as studying their magnetic properties using techniques like X-ray and
neutron scattering experiments as well as SQUID magnetometry.
Materials I focus on include metal oxyhalides, which cover a wide range of crystal structures
depending on your choice of metal and halide ions, and misfit layer compounds, which are layered
composite structures made up of two interpenetrating sublattices of different chemical composition,
which can be seen as naturally occurring heterostructures that combine distinct vdW layers with
complex stacking.[5]

Research Mission
We do fundamental research on heterogeneous catalysts and related nanomaterials to establish the relation between
structure and function on multiple length scales, ranging from the atomic level (nm) to the level of individual
catalyst particles (µm) and reactors (m). We aim to understand and improve the synthesis of solid catalysts and
sorbent materials and characterize them in detail during and after synthesis. We are especially interested in the
development of in-situ spectro-microscopic and tomographic multi-technique approaches to study porous
materials with sub-nanometre to micrometre resolution ex-situ, but also while they work under realistic
conditions (i.e., operando mode). Our research is connected to major societal and environmental developments.
We pursue the development of improved catalytic routes to arrive at a more sustainable supply of transportation
fuels, base and fine chemicals and functional materials (e.g., coatings), but also study the development of
sustainable routes for chemical recycling, biomass conversion, and solar fuels, as well as the study of the impact
of certain chemicals, such as micro- and nanoplastics, on the environment.

Sponsor: NWO, since November 2023
Supervisor(s): dr. Matteo Monai, prof. dr. ir. Bert Weckhuysen
Light stimulation, operando spectroscopy, CO2 hydrogenation
To make prospective sustainable technologies more economically feasible, a new way of catalyst
design is needed. Catalysts are now continuously improved by changing their composition and
nanostructure. However, there are boundaries to how active catalysts can be, because the interaction
of reaction intermediates with the catalyst must be balanced: not too strong and not too weak, but
just right. This is a compromise.[1] An emerging approach to overcome these boundaries is that of
resonant catalysis (RC). In RC, catalysts are stimulated by an intermittent stimulus, such as light,
mechanical stress or electric fields, at high frequency (Hz-MHz), in order to change the interaction
with reaction intermediates at the time scale of the reaction itself, so that the activity is not limited
by a specific step of the reaction. RC theory predicts an enhancement in catalytic performance up to
3 orders of magnitude above the maximum predicted by the well-known Sabatier principle (Figure
1).[2] Despite the promising RC predictions, only mild (up to 2 times) enhancement in catalytic activity 29
has been shown experimentally so far by intermittent stimulation, because the stimulus-catalyst
interactions are not well understood and the choice for stimulation parameters was so far based on
trial and error.[3]
Therefore, this project is focused on developing high time-resolution (up to 109 Hz, ns) operando
infrared (IR) spectroscopy tools, based on step-scan IR methods, to observe the effect of the
stimulation on catalysts at work. We will use light as a stimulus and focus on the CO2-to-methanol
(MeOH) reaction because of societal relevance and existing challenges in catalytic performance.[4]
We will determine the relationship between the light stimulation parameters, catalytic performance,
and the type and dynamics of the reaction intermediates formed during stimulated catalysis in the
CO2-to-MeOH reaction, to boost activity by a factor of 10 with respect to continuous illumination.

Thermo-Plasmonic Catalysis, Light-induced Assembly
Currently, in most catalytic processes entire reactor vessels are heated by burning fossil fuels,
resulting in various deactivating side-reactions and little spatial or temporal control over the reaction
processes. Preferably, just the catalytic surface where the chemical reactions take place is heated.
Locally delivering energy to the catalyst system requires complete redesign of the configuration
of a chemical reactor. In the CATlight consortium, we introduce the use of light to steer chemical
reactions where the catalytically active sites are locally heated by absorption of optical radiation.
Our proposed reactor design is composed of a vessel that is filled with a three-dimensional mesh
of optical waveguides/fibers that are decorated with plasmonic nano-heaters and catalyst particles.
Intense light pulses are guided through the 3D network and excite the plasmonic nanoparticles
thermally coupled to catalytic nanoparticles, while reaction gasses are continuously flowing through
34 the vessel. The use of electrically powered optical excitation makes the energy use more sustainable.
My work will be on smart assembly of these specifically tailored plasmonic/catalytic nanostructures
that can be used for thermo-plasmonic photocatalysis.[1,2] Smart assembly is required for precise
placement of the three components: 1) optical waveguides (dielectric optical waveguide/fiber micro/
nanostructures) that guide light to where it is desired, 2) plasmonic particles (e.g., Au, Ag, HfN) that
convert light into heat, and 3) catalytically active metal particles that use the localized heat to form
chemical products. Nano heater and catalyst particles will be grown on the optical waveguides using
either direct photochemical reduction of precursor solutions of metal salts (for both nano heater
and catalyst) or through colloidal deposition (nano heater) combined with photochemical reduction
(catalyst particles).[3,4] The prepared nanostructures will be employed in different catalytic reactions
with increasing complexity; starting with a prototypical heterogeneous reaction, CO oxidation. Later
expanding to more complex reactions: propane dehydrogenation, which is an endothermic reaction,
and dry methane reforming for which elevated temperatures are needed.

Waste accumulation in the environment is an urgent and multi-faceted problem. The diverse
approaches needed to tackle it include lowering the production of (single-use) plastic materials, and

50% of the global plastic production. Unfortunately, their traditional recycling approach of melting

monomers, that can be used in the chemical industry. For polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene

temperature needed to break the strong C–C bonds during thermal or catalytic cracking, random
bond scission, uncontrolled further reactions and thus the formation of branched, cyclized, and 37
aromatic hydrocarbons cannot be avoided.[1] Alternative strategies, possible at lower reaction
temperatures and with higher selectivity, promise a superior energy efficiency and control over
the product distribution. While thermal cracking of PE and PP starts above 355 °C, organic radicals
can form even at −196 °C when these polymers are exposed to mechanical force.[2,3] In that case,
mechanical strain lowers the vibrational energy needed for covalent bond scission, so that the
backbone bonds are not broken by thermal energy alone. In this project, we use a ball mill reactor to
combine mechano-chemical bond scission with heterogeneous catalysis to explore the mechano-
catalytic depolymerization of model and waste PP. While mechano-chemical bond cleavage is
usually undesired in plastic production, it here serves as a purposeful strategy for chemical recycling.

drive chemical conversions (Figure 1).

Catalysis operates on a broad range of pressures and temperatures, from ambient conditions to
temperatures above 1000 K, depending on the catalyst and reaction of interest. Small variations in
the overall reactor temperature are known to affect the catalytic performance. While local variations
in temperature likely play an equally important role, these are rarely studied in detail. To study local
heat effects in catalytic reactions, temperature measurements over a broad temperature range and
with a high spatial resolution are necessary. In this work, we use “luminescence thermometry” to
study local temperatures during catalytic reactions. Microcrystalline 1-µm-diameter yttrium oxide
particles doped with neodymium are mixed into the reactor bed. Neodymium emits near-IR light
with a temperature-dependent spectrum. We can thus determine local temperature variations by
mapping the neodymium emission spectrum. By tuning the neodymium doping concentration for
optimal signal strength, we achieve precise temperature readouts (error of <1 K) at temperatures 39
relevant for various catalytic processes. We characterized spatial temperature heterogeneities with
µm resolution during the exothermic carbon dioxide methanation reaction. We also characterized
cross-sensitivity of the measured signal to other parameters than temperature, such as light
absorption by the blackened sample due to coke deposition at elevated temperatures. Introducing
reaction gases causes a local temperature increase of the catalyst of on average 6–25 K, increasing
with the reactor set temperature in the range of 550–640 K. Pixel-to-pixel variations in the
temperature increase show a standard deviation of up to 1.5 K, which are attributed to local variations
in the catalytic reaction rate. Mapping and understanding such temperature variations are crucial for
the optimization of overall catalyst performance on the nano- and macroscopic scale.

nickel catalyzed (de)hydrogenation reactions, such as CO2 methanation. Most catalytic reactions are

tivity. The specific activity of surface atoms depends on their electronic structure and the atomic
arrangement in their surrounding (coordination). The electronic structure and atomic arrangement
are in turn influenced by the shape and size of the nanoparticle and can be tuned by the addition of
promoters or modifiers. To study structure sensitivity, nanoparticles with well-defined shapes and
sizes are thus necessary. In this project, nickel nanoparticles of several sizes and shapes will be syn-
thesized to selectively expose different surfaces. Additionally, the effect of addition of other metals

The synthesized nanoparticles will then be supported on high surface area supports and the catalysts
will be tested in, for example, CO2 hydrogenation, as a model structure sensitive reaction. The effect
of nanoparticle shape and promoters will be studied by operando techniques such as infrared and
X-ray absorption spectroscopy. This study is expected to give new fundamental insights in structure
sensitivity which will guide rational design to improve catalysts for(de)hydrogenation reactions.

with nickel. In addition, a reactor will be developed to demonstrate the performance of the activated
membranes.

metal catalyst at the atomic level. This aids in comprehending how the structural changes in the
catalyst, such as the reduction of copper oxide to metallic copper, the evolution of facets / crystalline
domains, influence the electrochemical conversion of CO2.
By studying CO2 electroreduction from these various perspectives, we aim to unravel the intricate
interplay between catalyst properties, intermediates, and the surrounding electrolyte. Our findings
not only contribute to the fundamental understanding of this important reaction but also offer
valuable insights for designing more efficient and selective electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion.

Mechanochemistry, Plastic Recycling, Radical Chemistry
I explore mechanochemistry, or causing chemical changes with mechanical instead of thermal energy
for recycling plastics. The current state-of-the-art recycling techniques are (1) mechanical recycling,
which melts down plastic and reshapes it and (2) chemical recycling, which breaks plastic down into
small building blocks either for making new plastic (repolymerization) or to be converted into other
useful chemicals (valorization). It is known from mechanical recycling that mechanically strained
polymers decrease in molar mass, indicating a chemical breakdown of the plastic. This phenomenon,
called mechanochemical recycling, has begun to be used to chemically recycle plastics, from
polyethylene terephthalate (PET) to polyolefins.[1,2] However, the mechanism of depolymerization of
polyolefins (polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS)) by mechanochemistry is
poorly understood. It has been proposed to proceed via a radical mechanism, where the mechanical
54 force causes carbon-carbon bonds to break in the middle, resulting in two carbon-centered radicals.
My research focuses on PP and PE degradation targeting their constituent monomers via ball mill
grinding. I explore the radical mechanism of the mechanochemical breakdown by introducing
radical trapping agents (Figure 1), such as spin traps and radical scavengers, to quantify and identify
radical species using spectroscopic techniques. I use electron spin resonance (ESR) and infrared
(IR) spectroscopies ex situ for bulk measurements at discrete timepoints. I am also exploring the
possibilities of an in situ milling jar with a transparent window for Raman spectroscopy.

dispersed metal catalysts (ADECs), which only provide isolated metal active sites with no crosstalk
between two neighboring metal atoms but strong chemical bonding interaction to the support. The
ultimate atomic efficiency as well as the unique electronic structure within the unsaturated coor-
dination of the atomically dispersed metal species is also distinct from its metallic nanoparticle
counterparts and has been shown to confer unprecedented catalytic properties. Using the strong
interactions between metals and defect-rich non-reducible supports, I explore various methods to
synthesize ADECs. Using them as model systems, I studied (a) the evolution of different active cen-
ters in catalytic conditions; (b) the dynamics and reactivity of isolated metal atoms, clusters, and
64 nanoscale particles (NPs); (c) the electromagnetic interactions and catalytic synergy among atoms
determined by the spatial positions of isolated atoms; (d) relay catalysis of isolated heteroatoms;
and (e) the correlation between catalytic reactivity and non-equilibrium oscillations of isolated at-
oms. A series of operando spectroscopies, including operando high-temperature and high-pressure
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), UV-visible
light absorption spectroscopy (UV-vis), and Raman spectroscopy, were employed to reveal the sur-
face dynamics of the working ADECs. Furthermore, I combined these spectroscopic results with ab
initio density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) to
achieve a fundamental understanding of catalytic reaction mechanisms at the atomic level. Building
upon these acquired insights, high-throughput screenings based on theoretical calculations were
employed to discover new catalytic materials with industrial potential for the selective hydrogena-
tion of CO2 and the selective oxidation of methane. The methodologies established for the operando
characterization and theoretical simulation of ADMCs have the potential to alleviate the ambiguity
surrounding the atomic-level comprehension of the catalytic mechanisms.

performance of this catalyst design will be evaluated, combined with an in-depth characterization

removed from alkene gas streams (e.g. propylene or ethylene). These impurities are detrimental for
product quality and cause severe deactivation of polymerization catalysts, and therefore have to be
removed from the alkene feed.

propylene-rich gas-stream. Traditionally, supported noble metals, such as palladium (Pd), have
proven to be very efficient hydrogenation catalysts. However, with high activity, selectivity can be
poor and over-hydrogenation to butane and propane may occur, especially when operating near full
butadiene conversion. For this process, the optimal catalyst retains a high selectivity to the butene 71
products, even close to full conversion of butadiene. Hence, in-depth understanding of selective and
non-selective processes is essential for the development of high-performance catalysts.

(noble) metal catalysts for the selective hydrogenation of butadiene in a 100-fold excess of propylene.
This includes rational synthesis design of supported catalysts, ranging from single atoms to large
nanoparticles. Fundamental studies into the genesis of the catalyst are performed with advanced
characterization methods such as STEM-EDX and operando EXAFS. Several catalytic structure-
performance relationships, such as the nanoparticle size[2], metal composition, support influence,
promoter effects and local concentration gradients are investigated under industrially relevant
reaction conditions.

The Nanophotonics group aims to control light, matter and their interactions at the nanoscale. Light-matter
interactions allow us to create and study extreme states of matter, ranging from quantum phenomena in space-time
crystals made of ultracold atoms, to transient electronic excitations in solids (e.g. exciton and its complexes), and
superheated plasmas in laser ablation. We develop and use methods to shape and measure the wavefront of light,
and use these in imaging, focusing and precise optical measurements as well as novel schemes for energy-efficient
optical information processing. With state-of-the-art ultrafast (in particular THz-based) spectroscopies, we
study the photophysics and many-body excitations in quantum materials for next-generation (opto-)electronics.
Precise optical measurements of nanoscale surface scattering allow us to detect processes of interest to biomedical
applications as well as study basic processes in energy storage materials.

In my research we are investigating and developing a novel spin-sensitive imaging method for
trapped quantum gases by incorporating digital off-axis holography with polarization-contrast

Quasicrystals constitute an intermediate phase between fully periodic and fully disordered media, in
which the positions of the atoms are perfectly ordered but not periodic. Such materials are relevant to
fundamental studies and for a wide range of applications, including spontaneous emission control,
lighting, photonic circuitry, photo-catalysis, and structural colors. The scattering properties of 3D
photonic quasicrystals differ vastly from these lower-dimensional systems and have so far been less
explored. Performing self-assembly of binary ensembles of nanoparticles in slowly drying emulsion
droplets (performed in the SCMB group) leads to equilibrium icosahedral quasicrystalline clusters,
which are approximately spherical.
In the case of a spherical sample, the scattering information is conveniently represented by the
scattering matrix in a basis of spherical harmonic waves. To measure the amplitude and phase of
96 scattered waves and find the scattering eigenstates of such samples, a holographic microscopy
approach is developed. The sample is illuminated by angle-scanning a laser beam. The multi-angle
scattered light is then received on a camera, where a reference beam enables amplitude and phase
detection. Measurements of the scattering properties give insights into the band structure and can be
used to further optimize the production of samples, aiming at a band gap for visible light.

In semiconductor device fabrication, a crucial step is quality control of the lithographic process.
An important metric in this process is overlay, which describes the error in alignment between
subsequent layers of the wafer. Currently, this is measured by printing designated ‘targets’ on the
empty spaces between printed circuits. These targets are then used to optically determine the overlay
and position of the layers. There are two problems with these targets. Firstly, the critical dimension
(size of the smallest features) of these targets is significantly larger than the critical dimension of the
structures in the chip itself. This causes a mismatch in the overlay error as measured by the targets
and the actual overlay error of the device. A second problem is the fact that the empty space between
chips is growing ever smaller as the space on a semiconductor wafer is pricey real estate, with recent
developments going as narrow as 40 microns. [1]
A way to solve these problems is by using on-chip alignment. Memory devices already employ this 97
strategy because of their periodic structure. Logic devices have a more complicated structure and
whether on-chip alignment is possible is still an open question. Since the structure of the chip is
fixed, we will optimize the shape of the incoming wavefront.
To determine the optimal shape of this wavefront we will use a framework based on Fisher [2] Fisher
information tells you how much information a random variable contains about some unknown
parameter. In this case the random variable is the incoming light, and the unknown parameter is the
overlay or some other property of interest. Using this framework, we can find states that have optimal
Fisher information, which means that using the right wavefront we can potentially determine the
quality of logic chip using on-chip alignment.

My research focuses on the innovative design of planar micro and nanoelectrodes using streamlined
and single-step methods. Our investigation delves into the electrochemical interactions between
these electrodes and solvated ions, employing optical AC-voltammetry—a specialized variant of
iontronic microscopy.
Diverging from conventional lithographic fabrication methods requiring cleanroom facilities, we opt
for laser ablation or origami techniques, enabling the rapid creation of micro and nanostructures
within seconds. In laser ablation, high-energy laser pulses selectively remove overlapping
disk-shaped regions from gold or single-layer graphene thin films, yielding sharp tips at their
intersections. These sharp tips facilitate the generation of a strong electric field gradient along their
surfaces.
Under the influence of an alternating electric field, solvated ions in the solution undergo 99
redistribution, creating a local refractive index contrast. We quantify this contrast using a
meticulously crafted total-internal reflection scattering microscope.[1] Unlike conventional methods
that rely on electrochemical analysis, our approach offers a comprehensive optical investigation
employing a sensitive differential imaging technique. The interferometric scattering signal from
internally reflected light carries crucial information on local refractive index changes due to ion
movement. To validate our proposed contrast mechanism, we cross-reference the optical ion signal
with concurrently measured electrical currents using a potentiostat.
Additionally, the inclusion of sharp corners and tips on the electrodes enables the trapping of
nanoparticles, augmenting their concentration within the field of view. Alternatively, we leverage
bendable conductive indium tin oxide (ITO) thin films on Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) to
fabricate origami nanoelectrodes, facilitating reversible particle trapping. Before the electric field
(Figure 3-a), particles show Brownian motion, while during its application, they localize at the
nanocrack (Figure 3-b); upon deactivation, they are promptly released (Figure 3-c). Through these
straightforward fabrication methods in conjunction with Iontronic microscopy, our research opens
avenues to scrutinize (electro)chemical interactions around nanoparticles at the single-particle level.

The synthesis of chemical building blocks and new organic compounds with interesting physical, biological, or
pharmaceutical properties remains as a challenge for the chemist. Recent and ongoing developments specifically
ask for ‘clean’ and efficient synthesis protocols, preferably based on renewable resources, to be developed for
current and future applications. Catalysis plays an important role in the development of such ‘clean’ and
sustainable synthetic protocols.
The OCC research group is actively involved with various aspects of catalysis. New organometallic and coordination
complexes are designed and synthesized in search of new catalytic properties in, e.g., oxidation catalysis, the
catalytic conversion of biomass, or catalysts for polymerizations. In the design of new catalysts and new catalytic
procedures the active sites of metallo-enzymes play an important inspirational role. In addition, new concepts in
ligand design are pursued, e.g. through the development of cooperative and dinucleating ligands, and the design of
ligands based on less traditional donor atoms like Si. Furthermore, research is done at the interface of organic and
inorganic chemistry, that is on the design of homogeneous as well as heterogeneous catalyst systems that will be
used in catalytic organic syntheses and the chemical transformation of renewable feedstocks, such as biomass, CO2
and recycling of waste streams.

recovered monomers are used to again form the polymers, having the same high quality material

would require excessive amounts of (scarce) renewable energy, as these are designed to be durable

space. However, fundamental understanding of the relationship between structure and function is
still lacking. Furthermore, some of the most promising examples lack a reasonable production route
from biomass.
The objectives of this project are to design biobased polyesters that are suitable for Chemical Recycling

structure-property relationships. For this, a machine learning methodology will be developed,

The great versatility of colloidal particles has made them one of the preferred building blocks for
assembling and studying complex structures at the microscopic level. In recent years the remarkable
ability to synthesize colloids with precise control over their shapes and interactions has endowed
them with directionality and shape anisotropy. These advancements enable precise control over
their assembly rules, resulting in the creation of novel crystal structures and complex molecules.
However, the interplay between shape and interaction that leads to crystal structures is not always
trivial, and the parameter space to be explored becomes significantly larger to be approached with
experiments.
Therefore, my research aims to develop and simulate models for these new complex systems and
to have an in-depth understanding of their self-assembly using molecular dynamics simulations.
120 Different interactions can be implemented using either: a) DNA-mediated interactions, where DNA
complementary strands are added to the surface of colloidal particles, thus creating directional
interactions, b) depletion interactions, where the addition of smaller particles, known as depletants,
to the system induces an effective attractive interaction between colloids, among others.
By using anisotropic colloids with the addition of the aforementioned interactions, we can control
the overall local and global structure of the system. For example, by increasing the concentration of
depletants on a system of tetrahedral particles with directional interactions,[1] we can go from a cubic
diamond crystal, to a percolating network with diamond inner structure, to a completely disordered
gel (see Figure 1). Thus, by accurately characterizing the space parameters in which the different
structures are found, they could serve as guides for experimental exploration.

dynamics that arises in glassy systems: Whilst quenching the system, we observe minimal structural
change, while simultaneously the dynamics slow down tremendously and become heterogeneous

In my PhD, we try to investigate the role that local structure plays in the development of this
heterogeneous dynamics. To do so, we use computer simulations of glassy systems, together
with machine learning (ML) techniques. Here, we build on previous research that has shown that,
although our human eyes see little to no structural change while quenching the system, computers
are in fact able to predict dynamical properties based on the local structure.[1][2][3] 121
One of the goals in the field of glassy machine learning is to improve these dynamical predictions,
which can be done in roughly two ways: on the one hand, one can use more suitable and complex
ML techniques, and on the other hand one can try to find parameters that better capture the input
data. In my PhD, I focus on the latter and try to develop more intelligent ways of capturing the local
structure of the glassy systems. Currently, with our newly found parameters, we are able to make
predictions for dynamical properties with a simple linear regression algorithm, that match the
predictions made by very complex graph neural networks.[4] Moreover, our hope is that these newly

pulsed excitation laser to study photon triplets emitted by individual quantum dots. More specifically,
I study the characteristic time delays between combinations of three photons. Three photons can be
emitted following three consecutive laser pulses (three excitons in separate laser pulses, Figure 1),
two laser pulses (a combination of a bi-exciton and an exciton during a separate laser pulse, Figure

visualized with a histogram of the delay times of two photons with regards to the third, Figure 5,

Structural color arises due to the interaction of refractive index differences with light. These
index differences can be formed by colloidal particles e.g. in light or different index solvents. More
specifically, structural color forms due to constructive and destructive interference with light. As such,
it has a longer lifetime and better chemical stability than pigment-based colors which deteriorate
or bleach over time. However, a common downside of structural colors is that the observed color
depends on the viewing angle.[1] This is due to the fact that Bragg scattering of a photonic lattice
depends on the orientation of the lattice w.r.t. the light. To get structural color that does not depend
on the viewing angle icosahedral supraparticles are synthesized, which have a spherically symmetric
regular 3D arrangement of colloids, resulting in an angle-independent color.[2]
What makes this work different from previous research is the incorporation of a responsive
component. This is achieved by self-assembling “rattle” particles, which consists of a core that can 125
move freely within a shell. To get switchable colors the cores of these rattle particles must consist
of a different dielectric material such that they can be positioned via an electric field. Meanwhile
the index of the solvent must match that of the surrounding shell such that these do not contribute
to scattering. When the cores are ordered under an electric field, constructive interference occurs,
yielding structural color. However, when the electric field is switched off, Brownian motion causes
the cores to become more strongly disordered (while the shells maintain their ordered geometry)
and the color to become much weaker.[3]

simple yet accurate coarse-graining framework may enable the characterisation, understanding,

Intelligent matter represents a cutting-edge field that merges materials science with artificial

stimuli but also internally adapt their structures, essentially possessing a form of intelligence.[1] This
form of intelligence, which involves the ability to obtain information, store it as knowledge, and
apply it to adjust behaviour in a dynamic environment, can be interpreted as learning. Due to their
adaptive behaviour, these materials would make manufacturing and engineering cheaper and more
sustainable.[2] The challenge lies in the vast data processing requirements inherent in advanced AI
applications, making centralized control of intelligent matter difficult. Traditional computers face
limitations in this regard, prompting the need for new computing paradigms implemented directly
at the material level.
Our focus lies in the exploration of the field wherein materials acquire knowledge through physical 127
experiences, this approach goes under the name of physical learning.[3] Unlike conventional computer-
based learning, this process involves exposing the material to examples of desired behaviour,
prompting changes in its components governed by a system-dependent dynamical process known
as a learning rule. This constitutes a decentralized, bottom-up approach to learning, distinct from
traditional computer methodologies. Recently, a theoretical and experimental application of one
such learning approach has been implemented in a network of variable resistors.[4] This network,
shown in the figure, has demonstrated the capability to execute tasks such as regression and image
classification.
We are currently advancing our efforts to optimize and customize this network. For instance, we are
exploring the possibility of incorporating memory-bearing elements, such as memristors, into the
system. Specifically, we are evaluating the potential integration of conical ion channels, which have
already demonstrated their applicability in neuromorphic computing.[5]

Quasicrystals are assemblies of particles that show a pronounced structural order, which is a typical
property of crystals. However, while conventional crystalline phases are characterized by repeated
unit cells periodically filling the whole space, quasicrystals do not have such translational symmetry.
Nonetheless, their structure can still be described by simple geometric shapes completely filling the
space in an aperiodic fashion, with specific rotational symmetries that may be forbidden for usual
crystals. The structural and physical properties of quasicrystals have earned them widespread
interest in applied sciences,[1] and the high complexity of their structure makes them an intriguing
and challenging playground for statistical mechanics.
While quasicrystals have been realized in a variety of metallic alloys, in soft matter they have only
recently been realized in a handful of different systems. On the simulation side, several studies have
been devoted to explore their self-assembly, but these often make use of interaction potentials that 137
are not easy to realize in colloidal experiments. Additionally, their formation process is still not well
understood.
A promising model system both for the experimental realization of colloidal quasicrystals and for
a fundamental investigation of their self-assembly consists of sedimented mono-layers of binary
mixtures of hard spheres. Such systems have been predicted to form two kinds of quasicrystals: one
with 8-fold and one with 12-fold rotational symmetry.[2]
My research project aims at understanding the entropy-driven process of formation of quasicrystals
through numerical simulations by looking at the dynamics of the local structural motifs formed
by neighboring particles. I also investigate other systems in which energetic interactions also play
a role, such as in directional bond-forming patchy particles, to understand if quasicrystal self-
assembly shares common features across completely different systems.

Since it was developed in the 1940s the Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory has
been highly successful in describing the phase behavior of charged stabilized colloids in solution.
However, it fails to explain experimental findings that suggest attractive interactions between
like-charged colloids, particularly in low-salt solutions. These phenomena include anomalous
behavior such as gas-liquid coexistence,[1] void formation in colloid suspensions [2] and long-lived
colloid crystals,[3] which are not accounted for in DLVO theory. Multiple theories have been proposed
that offer potential explanations for this behavior, which focus on effects related to many-body
interactions between colloids,[4] or related to regulation of the colloid surface charge.[5]
In my PhD project I investigate these colloidal like-charge attractions using simulations, which
model both the colloids and the electrolyte explicitly in which they are suspended. Phenomena such
as surface charge regulation and renormalization will also be included in these simulations. 141
However, though simulations of charged colloids can lead to more insight into like-charge attractions,
they have the downside of being extremely time-consuming, since the ions in suspension need to
be considered explicitly to capture the attractive interactions. To address this challenge, I employ
machine learning (ML) techniques to develop an effective coarse-grained many-body potential
between charged colloids, thereby eliminating the need to explicitly consider the ions in solution.
We fit these effective many-body potentials as a function of all colloid coordinates with a set of two-
body and three-body symmetry functions using a simple linear regression scheme. The use of these
ML potentials significantly accelerates the simulations. Moreover, investigating these potentials can
shed light on the intriguing ‘like-charge attractions’ observed between colloids in solution.

In the 1940s, Onsager showed that an isotropic (I) fluid composed of infinitely long rods exhibits an
entropy-driven first-order phase transition to a uniaxial nematic(N) phase.[1] In the nematic phase,
particles lack positional order but exhibit orientational order as they align preferentially along a so-
called nematic director. In experimental situations, when the liquid crystal sample is confined and
subject to anchoring conditions or external fields, it can be described by a continuous vector field,
which in turn might be accompanied by four basic modes of distortion: splay, twist, bend and saddle
splay.[2]
As early noted by Meyer,[3] when particles deviate from cylindrical symmetry things become
interesting. The particle deformation is locally enforced in the nematic director, but, without being
uniform in space, it induces a global frustration favouring either non-trivial couplings among the
144 modulations or even the spontaneous formation of discontinuities in the field called defects.
In this project, we investigate what kind of modulations and defect structures may be stabilised by
entropy alone. To this end we perform extensive simulations of hard particles of different shapes,
including bananas and tetrahedral rods.

As a sustainable, bio-based alternative to traditional pigments, my project focuses on replicating
structural colour in the lab through the self-assembly of cellulose nanocrystal (CNCs). These
colloidal particles are created by dissolving cotton in acid, and have a chiral shape, which results in
a cholesteric liquid crystal. This liquid crystal selectively reflects left-handed polarized light with a
wavelength dependent on the twisting power of the helical structure. Through drying suspensions 147
of CNCs we can freeze in the cholesteric crystal phase, resulting in colourful films, which could
potentially replace pigments in a variety of applications.
Currently, the films produced by the self-assembly of CNCs do not show uniform colour yet. Instead,
they are iridescent, meaning that the colour we see is dependent on the angle under which we view
the film. In order to negate this iridescence, we once again find our inspiration in nature. The beetle
Chrysina Gloriosa displays structural colour combined with a secondary structure of polygonal
domains in its carapace to ensure that the periodicity of the nanoscale layers is conserved under
varying viewing angle. Through magnetic manipulation of the CNCs we are currently working on
replicating this secondary structure to negate the iridescence, and come one step closer to utilizing
structural colour in real-world applications.

Inverse Design, Porous Materials, Self-Assembly
A zeolite is a common porous material widely employed in industry as a catalyst and adsorbent.
Despite its extensive use, the nucleation and growth mechanisms of zeolites in industrial synthesis
remain unclear, hindering the discovery of new zeolites. To address this, we aim to perform data-
based inverse design of diverse zeolite models using molecular dynamics simulations.
Our work is based on the Molinero Model[1], a binary coarse-grained model with tetrahedral-
forming T particles and structure-directing S particles. The T-T pairwise interaction employs the
Stillinger-Weber potential[2], including a two-body and three-body interaction term, to simulate the
tetrahedral interaction of silicon atoms. Various structures, such as the SGT zeolite framework, Z1
metal-organic framework, sII clathrate, and diverse mesophases, have been reported for this model.
Therefore, adjusting potential parameters makes it possible to reproduce other zeolite frameworks.
To achieve target zeolite frameworks, we develop an inverse design workflow with an ask-and-tell 149
interface, as shown in Figure 1a. The central component is the global optimizer, CMA-ES (Covariance
Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy), which searches for optimal interaction parameters and
thermodynamic conditions based on a fitness function. We speed-up the sampling by inserting a seed
of the target framework, thereby accelerating the nucleation events. We employ the environmental
similarity[3] as an order parameter to identify the target zeolite-like T particles. Subsequently, the
fraction of T particles that belong to the target zeolite is employed as the fitness value guiding the
optimizer. This cycle repeats until sufficient high-fitness solutions are found. We then perform a
self-assembly test to verify if the zeolite forms spontaneously from solution for the interaction
parameters and thermodynamic conditions that are optimized. Using this approach, we successfully
reverse-engineered the SOD framework, as depicted in Figure 1b. Our inverse design protocol
presents a robust tool for exploring new zeolite phases.

Research Mission
In the Van ‘t Hoff laboratory for Physical and Colloid Chemistry at Utrecht University the focus of our teaching and
research is on the physical chemistry of objects with sizes between a nanometer and several micrometers, the so-
called ‘colloidal scale’. Understanding the behavior of matter at the colloidal scale, where objects exhibit thermal
motion and ensembles can be described via thermodynamics, is important for many scientific disciplines including
biology, geosciences, physics, and engineering.
We create new colloidal model systems, engineer advanced materials, perform experiments with state-of-the-
art techniques, and develop new theory. Knowledge of the interactions and structure formation of matter at the
colloidal scale is crucial for the development of foods, coatings, electronic displays, and artificial drug and gene
delivery vehicles. There are ongoing national and international collaborations with academic groups and industry.
Our most applied topics of research include:
- Overcoming diffusion limitations for the ultrafast charging of lithium ion batteries
- Porous systems for nanofiltration, catalysis, and electrochemistry
- Magnetic fluids and their use in plastic waste separation
- Hybrid colloids for optical sensing
Our most fundamental research lines include:
- Structure formation and dynamics in well-defined colloidal dispersions in bulk and at interfaces
- Structural analysis of (photonic) colloidal crystals from X-ray scattering
- Thermodynamics of charged colloids and electrochemical interfaces
- Cooperative transitions in simple macromolecules
- Model systems for genetic regulation

Bijels, Interfacial Catalysis, Microfluidic Devices
In 2005 a new class of soft-materials consisting of two interpenetrating, continuous networks of
immiscible liquids was introduced.[1] These rigid structures are known as bicontinuous interfacially
jammed emulsion gels (bijels) which are stabilized by a jammed layer of colloidal nanoparticles
(NPs). Their high surface-area porous channel network, containing both an oil- and water phase and
the presence of NPs lead to potential applications in various areas like catalysis, separation mediums
and sensors. [1–4]
In this project, we will investigate the catalytic application of bijels as new type of industrial
reactor. Nowadays, the syntheses of chemicals and pharmaceuticals consume large amounts of
energy, leave toxic solvent waste behind and utilize over 15% of the global energy consumption to
purify the products.[5,6] Bijels can reduce this expenditure since the reaction and separation occur
154 simultaneously within one single step. Due to the different liquid polarities, both the reactants
and products can partition into one of the phases (figure 1). Furthermore, bijels can facilitate close
contact between immiscible reagents. This renders the use of organic solvent superfluous, making
catalytic bijels economically feasible too. [7, 8]
The main objectives of this project are to prepare, characterize and test catalytically active bijels.
Different NPs which can both stabilize the immiscible liquids and are catalytically active will be tested.
Preparation will be executed by the valuable method of solvent transfer induced phase separation
(STrIPS) using microfluidic devices to enable continuous fabrication of bijel fibers.[9, 10] Characterization
will be performed using confocal, optical and electron microscopy. Examples of industrial biphasic
reactions e.g. hydrolysis and esterification, will be tested in homogeneous and/or heterogeneous
conditions. A continuous flow reactor out of these bijels will be constructed using photolithography.
The flow of fluids throughout the pore network will be realized using an electroosmotic or pressure-
driven flow.

Bijels, Membrane Separations
As water scarcity poses a growing threat to several parts of the world, there is a pressing need to
increase our water supply through purification of unconventional water resources such as seawater.[1]
A common membrane-based technique to purify seawater for everyday use is desalination. The pore
size of these membranes is such that water molecules can pass the membrane, but hydrated salt ions
and other solutes are rejected. However, current membrane-based technologies are fundamentally
limited in their throughput. Separations requiring high selectivity, such as desalination, are
characterized by low permeabilities.
This project aims to employ bijels as templates for high specific surface area membranes in
order to increase the membrane permeate flowrates up to two orders of magnitude. Bicontinuous
interfacially jammed emulsion gels (bijels) can be prepared using a technique called solvent
156 transfer-induced phase separation (STrIPS).[2] In STrIPS, a mixture of water, oil and solvent
undergoes spinodal demixing upon solvent removal. In this demixing process, an interpenetrating
network of oil and water channels is formed. Coarsening of the network is arrested by adsorption
of nanoparticles onto the fluid-fluid interface. This results in a bicontinuous, porous material with
large internal surface areas up to 2 m2/cm3 .
In this project, we work towards the use of bijels in molecular separations in multiple steps. First of
all, the architecture and mechanical properties of bijels are tailored to overcome diffusion-limited
transport in the membrane. Moreover, we develop an approach to connect the channels of the bijels
to their respective bulk phases. Afterwards, a selective polymer layer is generated within the bijels
by interfacial polymerization. The results from this project contribute to our understanding of bijel
formation and pave the way to the use of bijels in molecular separation processes.

The cooling of buildings requires an enormous amount of energy, and due to climate change
cooling needs will increase.[1] Passive radiative cooling of buildings could be achieved by optimizing
the optical properties of the walls and roofs. If a surface radiates more energy (by way of infrared
radiation) than that it absorbs from solar irradiation, the surface will cool down.[2]
One highly reflective surface found in nature is the chitin shield of white scarab beetles.[3] The high
reflectance of the beetle shield has been shown to be a result of the optimized degree of anisotropy
in the interwoven structure of chitin filaments. This observation was confirmed by computational
studies and shown to be invariant of the exact topology of the structure.[4]
In our group a different interwoven structure is extensively studied. The structure that forms during
spinodal phase decomposition can be kinetically trapped through absorption of nanoparticles to
the interface, forming a bicontinuous interfacially jammed emulsion gel (bijel).[5,6] While these 157

of nanometers.[7] As a result, the material has a correlation length similar to the wavelength of visible

reflectance using anisotropic bijel structures. To make these, we consider two general strategies,
either post-processing the structure by stretching, or influencing the spinodal decomposition
dynamics using high aspect ratio nanoparticles in the synthesis process. By combining these methods
we aim to control the domain shapes, and by extension degree of anisotropy, of the bijels. We then
characterize both the structure and optical response of these bijels, thus allowing us to correlate the
correlation lengths and anisotropy of the structure to the total reflectance.

of a nanoparticle-stabilized network of two immiscible liquids. Bijels can be formed via solvent

by the rigidification of a layer of nanoparticles at the oil/water interface. This generates bijel

suitable structure for application as a separation membrane.

emulsification behavior in dependence of the changing liquid-liquid environment and complement
158 this by interfacial elasticity measurements on the particle adsorption at the oil/water interface. These

flat-sheet bijel membranes on a plastic substrate. Here, we investigate interfacial phenomena that
influence the microstructure of bijel films such as the substrate wetting. Last, we impart separation
selectivity to our bijel membranes via surface functionalization with polyelectrolyte multilayers
or thin polymer films. The combination of roll-to-roll synthesis and improved fundamental
understanding of STrIPS-bijel formation open avenues to realize the exciting application potentials
